scope: Calibration of the six circulating narratives about foreign capital in India — 'BlackRock and Vanguard own India's companies', 'the Rothschilds control the RBI / Indian banking', 'Soros, Hindenburg and OCCRP ran a coordinated campaign against Adani/Modi', 'FPI money is round-tripped Indian black money via Mauritius', 'the World Bank and IMF dictate Indian policy', 'Jio BlackRock got a fast-track licence' — plus two mirror narratives that circulate on the other side ('OCCRP is a US deep-state instrument' and 'SEBI's 2025 orders prove Hindenburg false'), each on the six-step ladder with strongest case, strongest counter, what would change it and opened sources. It records the documented record behind each narrative as claims: the Hindenburg reports of 2023-01-24 and 2024-08-10 as published by Hindenburg, the OCCRP investigation of 2023-08-31 as published by OCCRP, the Supreme Court's constitution of the expert committee and its 2024-01-03 judgment, the committee's May 2023 finding as quoted in the press, SEBI's final order of 2025-09-18 (opened and read), Adani Enterprises' exchange intimation of 2025-09-19, the Buchs' denial and the Lokpal's 2025-05-28 dismissal, the funders OCCRP itself lists and the Drop Site/Mediapart finding on its US-government share, George Soros's Munich remark and the BJP's responses (Feb 2023, Dec 2024), the RBI's own statement of its ownership, Rothschild & Co India's own description of its regulated business, the P-notes/ODI regulatory history (SIT 2015, SEBI 2016/2017) and the India–Mauritius treaty renegotiations (2016, 2024), one World Bank development-policy loan read for its conditionality, and the SEBI mutual-fund licence comparators reachable this session. It is the literature register for the capital fleet: every work listed in docs/research/CAPITAL_LITERATURE.md that was actually opened appears here as a node. It leaves out: named-holder percentages (holders.json), adviser mandates and the Jio BlackRock licence chronology itself (mandates-ventures.json, cross-referenced by claim id), FPI rule changes as a register (other file), World Bank project-level data (finance fleet), FCRA and Open Society grant flows to Indian associations (ngo fleet). Institutions, not bloodlines: 'the Rothschilds' and 'Soros' are handled only in narratives; the nodes are Rothschild & Co, its Indian subsidiary, Open Society Foundations, Hindenburg Research and OCCRP. The BJP's 31 Aug 2023 press conference on OCCRP/Soros could not be opened (bjp.org 503, BS/DH 403) and is recorded as a gap, not cited.

narratives.claim: BlackRock and Vanguard own India's companies.
narratives.strongestCase: BlackRock and Vanguard are the two largest asset managers on earth; BIS CGFS 66 documents that investment funds now channel more foreign capital to emerging markets than banks do and that passive index strategies move in herds; BlackRock has a 50:50 Indian AMC (Jio BlackRock) whose debut NFO raised Rs 17,800 crore; Vanguard is a named ≥1% holder in HDFC Bank (2.44%). Their combined benchmark-driven presence across every large Indian stock is real.
narratives.strongestCounter: Tested against primary SEBI shareholding-pattern filings (holders.json), BlackRock/iShares is a named ≥1% shareholder in 0 of 5 NIFTY 50 constituents opened (Reliance, HDFC Bank, ITC, Bharti Airtel, SBI); Vanguard in 1 of 5; the Norwegian and Singaporean sovereign funds in 2 of 5 each; LIC — Indian, state-owned — is the largest non-promoter holder in 3 of 5. The foreign stakes that actually confer influence are strategic (BAT 22.91% of ITC; Singtel 7.49% of Bharti Airtel), not passive. An index fund votes its clients' benchmark weight; it does not own or direct. 45 constituents remain unchecked.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Named-holder data for all 50 constituents showing BlackRock or Vanguard at ≥5% in a material number, or any board seat, voting agreement or promoter-group classification; conversely, full-index data confirming the five-company pattern would move this to 'debunked'.

narratives.claim: The Rothschilds control the RBI / Indian banking.
narratives.strongestCase: Rothschild & Co is a real, active adviser in India (SEBI merchant banker since 1998; '145 M&A deals since 2010' by its own count; ranked no. 3 by deal count 2007–2023 in Forbes' tally per mandates-ventures.json), and the name carries two centuries of documented banking power, which Ferguson's history confirms was genuine in the 1820s–1870s.
narratives.strongestCounter: The RBI states on its own site that it has been 'fully owned by the Government of India' since nationalisation in 1949, with a board appointed by the Government under the RBI Act 1934. Rothschild & Co's entire Indian presence is one advisory subsidiary with no banking licence, no lending, no asset management and no disclosed shareholding in any Indian bank; it is absent from every named-holder filing and every LSEG H1 2024 top-10 opened by the sibling files. The 'control' trope has a documented propaganda lineage — the fictional Waterloo legend, Dairnvaell's 1846 pamphlet, Nazi propaganda — and the family's wealth has been divided among many descendants; scholars class the control claim as an antisemitic canard. Under this project's rules a family is not an actor; the institutional referent has been checked and found to be a mid-sized adviser.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Any primary record of a Rothschild entity holding a banking licence, an RBI or PSU-bank board seat, or a disclosed ≥1% stake in an Indian bank. None exists in any opened source.

narratives.claim: Soros, Hindenburg and OCCRP ran a coordinated campaign against Adani/Modi.
narratives.strongestCase: Documented components: (1) Open Society Foundations is one of OCCRP's 26 listed institutional funders; (2) George Soros said at Munich on 16–17 Feb 2023 that Adani's troubles would 'significantly weaken Modi's stranglehold on India's federal government'; (3) Hindenburg published on 24 Jan 2023 with a disclosed short position and again on 10 Aug 2024 against the SEBI chair; (4) OCCRP, the Guardian and the FT published a documents-based follow-up on 31 Aug 2023 naming two Adani associates; (5) the US government supplied ~52% of OCCRP's spending 2014–23 (Drop Site/Mediapart, Dec 2024); (6) the Lokpal (May 2025) described Hindenburg as 'a known short seller trader whose focus was to expose or corner Adani Group'. A common funder, a shared target and a shared political reading are all on the record.
narratives.strongestCounter: No document in any opened source links Soros/OSF to Hindenburg — Hindenburg's investors are undisclosed, and the claim that Soros is its 'main investor' has never been sourced. OSF is one of 26 OCCRP funders with an unpublished share, and the larger documented funder is the US government. The OCCRP piece came seven months after Hindenburg's and rests on bank and tax-haven records that neither Adani nor SEBI has shown to be forged; the Supreme Court in Jan 2024 held such reports insufficient as proof, not false. SEBI's Sept 2025 orders found the two RPT strands 'not established' — a finding about Adani's conduct, not about coordination among its accusers. Common funders and simultaneous interest in the same target are the base rate for investigative journalism about any conglomerate; 'coordination' as a directed campaign requires a communication, a payment or an instruction, and none has been produced. The symmetry check (below) shows the same lens paints the pro-Buch response of Aug 2024 as equally 'coordinated'.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a grant, contract or correspondence showing OSF or a government funder commissioned the Adani story or funded Hindenburg; a SEBI/court finding that Hindenburg traded on non-public information supplied by OCCRP or vice versa. Down/kill: SEBI's remaining FPI strand sustaining the OCCRP allegation on the merits, which would make the 'campaign' a correct exposure rather than a fabrication regardless of funding.

narratives.claim: FPI money is round-tripped Indian black money via Mauritius.
narratives.strongestCase: The structure is documented by the state itself: over a third of FDI into India 2000–2015 came through Mauritius, a jurisdiction with no capital-gains tax; the Union renegotiated the treaty in 2016 (source taxation from 1 Apr 2017) and again in 2024 (principal-purpose test explicitly against 'treaty shopping'); the SC-appointed SIT on black money in 2015 treated ODIs (Rs 2.715 lakh crore outstanding) as a laundering risk and demanded beneficial-owner identification; SEBI tightened ODIs in 2016 and 2017 and imposed look-through disclosure on concentrated FPIs in Aug 2023 after Hindenburg alleged exactly this mechanism for Adani; the OCCRP documents show two Mauritius funds taking instructions from a Vinod Adani-linked adviser.
narratives.strongestCounter: No official document has ever quantified the round-tripped share: the SIT recommended, SEBI regulated, but nobody published a numerator. Treaty shopping is the rational choice of every non-resident investor, so the Mauritius route's size measures tax arbitrage, not residency. ODIs fell from a 2007 peak to a small fraction of FPI assets after the 2007, 2016 and 2017 measures (the exact series was not opened). The named ≥1% foreign holders actually found in five NIFTY 50 filings are sovereign funds and SEC-registered index managers that publish their own holdings. On the one case where the allegation was specific (Adani), SEBI's finished strands found nothing established and the SC declined to treat the OCCRP documents as proof.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Publication by SEBI of the Aug 2023 look-through results by ultimate beneficial-owner residency; a court or ED finding attributing a specific FPI/ODI book to Indian residents; or, in the other direction, those results showing Indian-resident BOs at a negligible share.

narratives.claim: The World Bank and IMF dictate Indian economic policy.
narratives.strongestCase: Development-policy operations carry 'prior actions' and forward triggers negotiated with Bank staff; US$2.75bn of 2020 budget support arrived at a moment of fiscal stress (finance/worldbank.json narrative 0); India borrowed under IMF programmes in 1981 and 1991, and the 1991 conditionality is the origin of the liberalisation reforms.
narratives.strongestCounter: The one DPO read here (P173943, US$750m, 30 Apr 2020) finances the Government's own already-announced PMGKY package; the finance fleet's read of 26 prior actions across three DPOs finds every one was a GoI measure announced or legislated before appraisal. India has had no IMF programme since 1991 (finance-fleet documented void; imf.org is blocked from this environment, so not independently re-verified here), its public debt is rupee-denominated and domestically held, and World Bank commitments are a small fraction of a Rs 45-lakh-crore Union budget. Conditionality on programmes the borrower already announced is a financing device, not dictation.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A DPO or IMF document whose prior actions were not previously announced GoI policy, or a documented instance of the Government reversing a stated policy to unlock a tranche; the finance fleet's register is the place to look.

narratives.claim: Jio BlackRock got a fast-track SEBI licence because of the Ambani connection.
narratives.strongestCase: Final registration came 7.7 months after in-principle approval, against ~19 months for Bajaj Finserv and (per unopened press dates) ~21 months for Angel One and ~23 for Zerodha; three Jio BlackRock licences (MF, investment adviser, broker) landed within five weeks in May–June 2025; the sponsor, Jio Financial Services, was under two years old as a listed entity when it applied, and reg. 7 was amended four months before its filing.
narratives.strongestCounter: On the in-principle leg — where sponsor fitness is actually judged — Jio BlackRock took 11.5 months, the same as Bajaj Finserv's 11; the June 2023 reg. 7 amendment applied to every applicant; the co-sponsor is the world's largest asset manager with a prior Indian AMC (DSP BlackRock, exited 2018), so operational readiness for the final leg is expected; press reporting (sibling file) records SEBI speeding approvals for all new entrants from 2023; SEBI publishes no processing-time statistics, so the comparator set is hand-built from press dates and two of the five comparators' in-principle dates could not be opened. No document shows any instruction, departure from checklist or contact that would make this favour rather than speed.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: SEBI's file or an RTI showing a departure from the standard checklist or a prioritisation instruction. Down: SEBI publishing 2023–25 durations showing 6–9-month final legs as the norm for well-capitalised sponsors.

narratives.claim: OCCRP is a US 'deep state' instrument used to destabilise India (BJP, Dec 2024).
narratives.strongestCase: Documented: the US government supplied 52% of OCCRP's spending 2014–2023 (46% on OCCRP's own basis) and at least US$47m since 2008; a USAID official confirmed the agency reviews and approves nominees for grant-funded 'key personnel' posts; OCCRP's coverage of US corruption has been minimal; the US indictment of Gautam Adani (Nov 2024) landed while OCCRP's Adani reporting was live.
narratives.strongestCounter: Government funding of investigative journalism in weak-philanthropy regions is the sector's norm and OCCRP publishes its funder list; its grants carry written editorial-independence clauses, its board says no donor has ever vetoed a hire or a story, and the US State Department denies editorial influence; the Adani story was a collaboration with the Guardian and the FT on bank records nobody has shown to be false; and a state that wished to 'destabilise' India would not be simultaneously its largest defence and technology partner. The claim conflates a documented funding dependency with an undocumented direction.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A US-government communication requesting, reviewing or timing the Adani story; or, the other way, OCCRP publishing audited per-funder figures and the Adani project's specific funding source.

narratives.claim: SEBI's 2025 orders and the Supreme Court gave Adani a 'clean chit' and proved Hindenburg false.
narratives.strongestCase: The SC-appointed committee (May 2023) found prima facie no regulatory failure; the SC (Jan 2024) refused a CBI/SIT transfer, upheld the FPI rule changes, dismissed conflict allegations and ordered a probe into Hindenburg itself; SEBI's final orders of 18 Sep 2025 found the Milestone/Rehvar and Adicorp allegations 'not established' and disposed of them 'without any direction'; the Lokpal dismissed the complaints against the SEBI chair as vexatious. Hindenburg closed in Jan 2025.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Sept 2025 orders decide two of 24 investigations on a legal point — that transactions routed via unrelated parties were not 'related party transactions' under the LODR as it stood in 2018–19 — and the SC judgment is expressly not a merits adjudication ('does not inspire confidence' is a holding on the petitioner's evidence). The FPI beneficial-ownership strand that OCCRP's documents bear on was not among the orders opened, and the US SEC/DOJ matters (energy fleet) are independent of Hindenburg. A finding that a specific allegation is 'not established' under a regulation is not a finding that the underlying facts (loans, offshore funds, instructions) did not occur; the order itself records that the loans were made and repaid.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: SEBI's order on the FPI beneficial-ownership strand, whichever way it goes; any appellate reversal at SAT; the outcome of the SC-ordered probe into Hindenburg.

symmetryCheck: Three lenses were run on the controls named in the brief and on the mirror side. (1) 'Foreign holder owns X' — applied to Vanguard, NBIM, GIC, Capital Group, Fidelity and LIC on the same five primary filings (holders.json): the sovereign funds of Norway and Singapore cross 1% twice as often as BlackRock (which never does), and the domestic state insurer LIC crosses 1% in four of five — the lens, applied evenly, produces 'Norway and Singapore own India' or 'the Indian state owns India' before it produces 'BlackRock owns India'; the narrative selects its actor. (2) 'Foreign adviser controls X' — applied to Lazard, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Kotak, Axis, Avendus (mandates-ventures.json): Rothschild & Co is absent from every LSEG H1 2024 top-10 where Citi, Kotak and Goldman appear, so the same lens run on the controls produces a more 'alarming' picture for Citi than for Rothschild; the narrative again selects its actor. (3) 'Coordinated foreign-funded campaign' — the identical test (common funder + same-week statements + shared target + political reading) applied to the response to Hindenburg's Aug 2024 report shows AMFI (the regulated industry), the Adani Group, a BJP office-holder, a senior lawyer, a former Infosys CFO and India's then IMF executive director issuing mutually reinforcing statements within 48 hours, carried by the state broadcaster (newsonair.gov.in) — which under the same lens is 'coordination' by state-funded media of a state-aligned message. Neither side's simultaneity is evidence of direction; both are the base rate of public controversy. The lens produces an equally alarming picture for the controls in all three cases; that is a finding about the lens, and the narratives are calibrated accordingly (unsupported/debunked for the actor-selecting claims; contested only where a documented structure exists without a numerator — Mauritius round-tripping — or where the record is genuinely two-sided — OCCRP's US funding, the 'clean chit').
